source: Irving, Szegedy, Alemi, Een, Chollet, Urban (2016) DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection
finding: First deep-learning premise selection on Mizar. Ranking premises with CNNs lets the E prover solve more theorems than a k-NN baseline at small premise budgets. Perfect premise choice is the upper bound the paper aims at.
numbers: Test set 2,742 theorems. At top-16 cutoff: k-NN 24.6%, char-CNN 25.1%, word-CNN 25.9%, def-CNN 26.8%, def+char-CNN 30.5%. At cutoff 1024: k-NN 65.1%, def-CNN 66.4%, def+char 67.9%.
quote: with perfect premise selection ATPs can prove at least 56% of Mizar and Flyspeck instead of today's 40%
limits: Gap to k-NN shrinks as the cutoff grows (65.1 vs 67.9 at 1024). Gains are largest when the budget is small. Single corpus (Mizar), E prover only.
agent_relevance: The value of a selector is largest when the context budget is tight. Our subgoal library needs a small top-k, so ranking quality matters most there.

source: Irving et al. (2016) DeepMath, negative mining and ensembles
finding: Hard-negative mining was crucial. Different models solve different theorems, so unions help a lot.
numbers: Negative mining doubled theorems proved at top-16. Union over all cutoffs for best neural model rose 61.3% to 66.4%. Union def-CNN + char-CNN 69.8%; def-CNN + k-NN 74.25%; all methods 80.9% (2,218 theorems); neural only 78.4%.
limits: Union numbers pool many runs, so they cost more compute than any single run.
agent_relevance: Use several retrieval signals (lexical plus learned) and take the union. Mine near-miss library items as negatives when we learn a retriever.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) Learning-Assisted Automated Reasoning with Flyspeck
finding: Learned premise advice plus many ATP strategies proved 39% of 14,185 Flyspeck theorems in 30 s using only earlier theorems and proofs. With true HOL Light dependencies the rate is 50%, and 56% over all experiments.
numbers: 39% of 14185 theorems (honest chain, 30 s, parallel). 50% with proof dependencies. Union of all experiments 56.5% with Isabelle, 54.7% without. Single best method 29.4% to 31.9% after a refinement step.
limits: Needs many ATP runs in parallel; the 39% is a portfolio number, not one method.
agent_relevance: A 11-17 point gap between learned advice and oracle advice shows how much headroom retrieval quality still has.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) Flyspeck, premise count versus prover
finding: Provers degrade when given too many premises. A second-stage filter (SInE) offsets some selector error.
numbers: Z3 drops from 12.4% (256 premises) to 6.2% (740). Vampire 18.1% to 12.9%. E-parallel stays above 20% at 512 premises and falls to 15.6% at 2048.
quote: 512 premises seems to be the current margin of error for the first-stage premise selection
limits: Specific to 2014 provers; neural prover context limits differ.
agent_relevance: More retrieved items is not free. Two-stage selection (broad recall, then filter) is a proven pattern for our library lookup.

source: Alama, Heskes, Kuhlwein, Tsivtsivadze, Urban (2014) Premise Selection for Mathematics by Corpus Analysis and Kernel Methods
finding: Learning from minimal proof dependencies plus a kernel method (MOR) beats Vampire/SInE heuristic pruning on 2,078 Mizar problems by about 50%.
numbers: Vampire/SInE auto mode 548 problems. SNoW-60: +32%; MOR-70: +45%. Combined runs +44% and +50% over 548. Recall in top 50: MOR 88%, SNoW about 80%.
limits: Gain is over a heuristic baseline on Mizar; combining two selection strategies inside Vampire was not productive.
agent_relevance: Learned relevance from past proofs beats syntactic heuristics. Suggests logging which library items past solutions used.

source: Alama et al. (2014) minimal dependency analysis
finding: Training on minimal dependencies (the smallest premise set that still proves it) gives cleaner labels than raw proofs.
numbers: Benchmark of 2078 problems. One setup solves 1105 problems, 8% over heuristic pruning.
limits: Label quality effect not isolated as one clean number in the sections read.
agent_relevance: Store minimal useful items per solved problem, not everything touched.

source: Alemi et al. (2017) HolStep
finding: Dataset for useful-step classification. Context on the conjecture barely helps; a context-free classifier gets nearly the same accuracy.
numbers: Unconditioned: logistic regression 0.71; 1D CNN 0.82-0.83; CNN-LSTM 0.77-0.83. Conditioned (Siamese): 0.71, 0.81-0.82, 0.77-0.83. Chance 0.5.
quote: Conditional and unconditional selection have similar performances
limits: Only 0.8% of statements appear as both positive and negative, so the test rewards statement-only cues (upper bound 97% unconditional per b08).
agent_relevance: Benchmarks can be solved by statement popularity, not relevance to the goal. Test our retriever on goal-conditioned cases.

source: Wang, Tang, Wang, Deng (2017) Premise Selection for Theorem Proving by Deep Graph Embedding (FormulaNet)
finding: Graph embedding of formulas raises HolStep accuracy from 83% to about 90%. Much of the signal still comes from symbol names.
numbers: Conditional 90.3%, unconditional 90.0% (prior best 83%). Zero update steps already 81.5%. Deepwalk topology-only 61.8%. Unconditional upper bound 97%. Variable renaming causes a very large drop for name-using models.
limits: HolStep usefulness labels; renaming test shows overfitting to name bias.
agent_relevance: Learned selectors may latch onto surface names. Rename or paraphrase probes can expose this in our library lookup.

source: Piotrowski, Fernandez Mir, Ayers (2023) Machine-Learned Premise Selection for Lean
finding: Random forest and k-NN with name and bigram features give working in-Lean premise selection. Random forest usually beats k-NN. Trigrams overfit.
numbers: Easy 'all premises' filter: random forest Cover 0.56 (0.67 Cover+), 0.57 with names+bigrams; k-NN 0.51-0.52. Trigram variants lower (0.47 forest).
limits: The 'all' filter has many easy examples, so its higher numbers are not comparable to stricter filters.
agent_relevance: Cheap non-neural selectors with name features are a strong baseline for a small library.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor: Wielding Hammers to Integrate Language Models and Automated Theorem Provers
finding: Language models are poor at choosing premises from a library. Outsourcing selection to Sledgehammer raises success more than the union of the two tools.
numbers: PISA test: LISA 33.2%, Sledgehammer 25.7%, language model 39.0%, union 48.8%, Thor 57.0%. Steps with premises advance the proof in 1.9% of cases versus 28.2% for steps with no premises. miniF2F 29.6% to 29.9%.
limits: Premise-step 1.9% vs 28.2% is a diagnostic, not a controlled test. miniF2F gain is tiny.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that free-form recall of library items is the weak point. Add an external lookup step rather than trusting the model to remember.

source: Mikula et al. (2024) Magnushammer, ICLR
finding: A transformer retriever with contrastive training and a rerank stage beats Sledgehammer and lexical and generic-embedding baselines.
numbers: PISA single-step: BM25 30.6%, TF-IDF 31.8%, OpenAI ada-002 embeddings 36.1%, Sledgehammer 38.3%, Magnushammer 59.5%. miniF2F test: Sledgehammer 10.4%, with heuristics 20.9%, Magnushammer 34.0%. With Thor: 57.0% to 71.0% (PISA).
limits: Equal-budget comparison needs an assumed CPU conversion; Sledgehammer budget hard to estimate. miniF2F multi-step 37.3% still below DSP 39.3%.
agent_relevance: Trained retrieval beats lexical match by wide margins, but generic embeddings only match the symbolic tool.

source: Mikula et al. (2024) Magnushammer ablations
finding: Small data and small models already beat Sledgehammer. Pretraining helps most when data is scarce.
numbers: 0.1% of data (about 4K samples) beats Sledgehammer. A 920K-parameter model reaches 40.7% vs 38.3%. Full data: 56.3% (MAPL) vs 54.0% (HPL). A 38M model SELECT-only reaches 54.2% vs 56.3% with rerank.
limits: Scaling layers helped more than embedding width; rerank adds about 2 points.
agent_relevance: A small retriever tuned on a modest set of solved cases may be enough for our library.

source: Mikula et al. (2024) Magnushammer false negatives
finding: Training data from human proofs alone mislabels useful premises as negatives, since other valid proofs exist. Adding Sledgehammer-made alternative proofs reduces this.
numbers: Human-only HPL gives 54.0% against 56.3% with the augmented MAPL set on full data.
limits: Effect size is small after pretraining.
agent_relevance: Absence from one known solution does not mean irrelevant. Do not punish unused-but-valid library items.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo / ReProver
finding: Retrieval of accessible premises helps a tactic-generating LLM, and the gain holds on theorems with premises never seen in training.
numbers: Pass@1 random split: tidy 23.8, GPT-4 29.0, ReProver 51.2, no retrieval 47.6. novel_premises split: tidy 5.3, GPT-4 7.4, ReProver 26.3, no retrieval 23.2. miniF2F 26.5%, ProofNet 13.8%.
limits: Retrieval adds only 3.6 and 3.1 points over no retrieval. GPT-4 baseline may be contaminated. Absolute novel-premise rate is half the random rate.
agent_relevance: Retrieval gain is real but modest; the split that needs new items is the hard one, which is our use case.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo retriever metrics
finding: Restricting search to accessible premises and adding in-file hard negatives improve retrieval. All methods fall on novel premises.
numbers: Random split R@1/R@10/MRR: BM25 6.7/17.2/0.15; ReProver 13.5/38.4/0.31; with all premises 11.7/36.2/0.27; without in-file negatives 10.8/33.1/0.25. novel_premises: BM25 5.9/15.5/0.14; ReProver 9.1/27.6/0.24. Accessible filter cut candidates from 128K to 33K.
limits: Recall@10 under 40% means the right item is usually missing; the prover still works with partial recall. LeanHammer notes their R@k definition differs.
agent_relevance: Filter the library by what is usable at this point (scope) before ranking. Even good retrievers miss most needed items, so keep a fallback.

source: Cross-check of lexical baselines: Mikula et al. (2024) and Yang et al. (2023)
finding: Across two benchmarks, plain BM25 is weak, and the order BM25 < generic embedding < trained retriever is consistent.
numbers: LeanDojo BM25 R@10 17.2 vs trained 38.4. PISA BM25 30.6 vs ada-002 36.1 vs trained 59.5.
limits: Different benchmarks and metrics; consistency is of order only.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on keyword or generic-embedding search alone.

source: Zhu, Clune, Avigad, Jiang, Welleck (2026) Premise Selection for a Lean Hammer (LeanPremise), ICLR
finding: A premise selector trained for hammer use beats MePo and a retrained ReProver. Neural and symbolic selectors solve different goals.
numbers: Mathlib-test: no selector 16.9% (full); MePo 19.1; ReProver 218M 12.0 (full), 22.3 (cumul); LeanPremise 82M recall@32 72.7%, full 30.1, cumul 33.3. Union with MePo: 35.9 full, 37.6 cumul. Ground-truth premises 41.0 / 43.0.
limits: Authors retrained ReProver on their splits. Gap to ground truth stays about 10 points.
agent_relevance: Combine learned and rule-based selectors. Selection tuned to the downstream tool (whole proof, not next step) matters.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) LeanPremise ablations and scaling
finding: Training details change results: data extraction, sampled negatives, loss masking. Model size helps modestly.
numbers: Recall@32 67.8% to 72.7% from 23M to 82M; full proof 27.9 to 30.1. Accumulating across sizes 34.5. Ablation on Mathlib-valid (medium model): removing the loss mask lowers recall@32 to 59.5; naive data extraction lowers it to 66.8; no negatives 71.9.
limits: One ablation (no loss mask) raised cumul proof rate; authors call it noise. Proof rate noisier than recall.
agent_relevance: Recall is a steadier metric than solve rate for tuning our lookup.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) LeanHammer failure analysis
finding: Most failures are in translation and the external prover, not selection.
numbers: Two settings: 21.7% (26.7%) not translated; 43.6% (50.4%) translated but not proven; 1.6% (1.2%) prover proof not reconstructed; 33.1% (21.3%) succeeded.
limits: The two columns refer to two settings in the appendix.
agent_relevance: Good selection is necessary, not sufficient. Check whether retrieved items are usable in the form our reasoning step needs.

source: Combining Textual and Structural Information for Premise Selection in Lean (2025)
finding: Adding graph neural network embeddings over the premise dependency graph improves a ReProver-style retriever.
numbers: LeanDojo test: R@1 17.98% (+33.98%), R@10 50.04% (+26.36%), MRR 0.4095 (+24.73%) over ReProver. Ablating context graph R@10 49.99 vs 48.52 with no ablation; premise graph ablation 49.30.
limits: Ablation differences are about 1 point. Relative gains stated against ReProver baseline; short paper.
agent_relevance: Links between library items (what depends on what) add some signal beyond text.

source: Gao et al. (2026) LeanSearch v2: Global Premise Retrieval for Lean 4
finding: Retrieving the whole premise set for a theorem, with sketch-retrieve-reflect loops, beats per-step selectors. Better retrieval carries over to proving.
numbers: nDCG@10 0.62 vs 0.53 next best. MathlibMPR (69 queries): group recall@10 46.1% vs 38.0% reasoning retrievers vs 9.3% premise-selection baselines. Prove with Claude Sonnet 4.5, 8 rounds: FATE-H n=100 no retrieval 4%, LeanFinder 12%, INF-X 7%, v2 standard 16%, v2 reasoning 20%. MathlibMPR-Prop n=50: 2 / 5 / 5 / 5 / 7 solved.
limits: Small n (50 and 100); differences of 1-3 problems. Authors built both benchmark and system.
agent_relevance: Letting the reasoner draft a sketch first, then retrieve, then revise queries, fits our loop and gives the best retrieval. Gains are small in absolute terms.

source: Ji (2026) CSLibPremiseBench
finding: A structure-aware reranker gives little over BM25 plus symbol match on a computer-science Lean library, and the labels are partly wrong.
numbers: 801 tasks, 1875 candidates. MRR CSG-Rerank 0.5236 vs BM25 0.5061 (diff +0.0175, 95% CI +0.0016 to +0.0335); vs BM25+symbol diff +0.0037 (CI -0.0103 to +0.0173). Recall@10 not improved. Strict audit keeps 2666/2845 proxy links (93.7%); elaborated check confirms 462/958 (48.2%).
limits: Proxy labels from source text. Single author, no downstream proving.
agent_relevance: Fancy structure may not beat cheap lexical plus symbol overlap in small domain libraries. Label noise limits measured gains.

source: Song, Yang, Anandkumar (2025) Lean Copilot
finding: Putting a retrieval-based premise selector inside Lean next to an LLM tactic generator and proof search automates most steps.
numbers: On Mathematics in Lean theorems: Aesop 40.1% of steps; suggest-tactics 58.3-58.4%; search-proof 74.2%. Fully autonomous: search-proof 63.7% (107/168).
limits: Totals are for the combined tool, not an isolated premise-selection ablation.
agent_relevance: Premise lookup is useful as one tool among several, not alone.

source: Dai et al. (2025) ProverQA: Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation
finding: Irrelevant facts mixed into the given premises lower GPT-4o accuracy, and shuffled order lowers it again, most on hard problems.
numbers: GPT-4o CoT, easy/medium/hard: default (distractions, shuffled) 94.2/79.4/50.0; no distractions 94.4/82.2/57.4; no distractions and ordered 95.6/87.4/62.4.
limits: Synthetic first-order logic stories, one model. Effect small on easy problems. Author attribution not checked.
agent_relevance: Extra, unneeded items cost real accuracy on hard problems, so precision of the selected set matters, and ordering by reasoning chain helps.

source: DRIFT (2025) Decompose, Retrieve, Illustrate, then Formalize Theorems
finding: Per a search summary only: on miniF2F, dependent-premise retrieval adds little and extra retrieved context mostly distracts. Not read in full.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified secondhand summary.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks where few premises are needed hide the value of retrieval; judge retrieval on premise-heavy tasks.

source: HybridProver (2025)
finding: Per a search summary only: training with premises cut undefined-fact errors in Isabelle by about half but did not improve miniF2F, where most theorems need no external premises. Not read in full.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified secondhand summary.
agent_relevance: Same caution: the benefit of premise help appears only when problems need library items.

source: Cross-study synthesis of b01-b24
finding: Pattern across 2014-2026 studies: trained selectors beat lexical and heuristic ones; learned and symbolic selectors are complementary; oracle premises set a ceiling 10-17 points higher; recall at small k drives results; too many or irrelevant items hurt.
numbers: Oracle gaps: Flyspeck 39% vs 50-56%; LeanHammer 33.3% vs 43.0%; DeepMath perfect-selection bound 56% vs 40% at the time. Retrieval over no retrieval: ReProver +3.6/+3.1 points; LeanSearch v2 4% to 20% (n=100).
limits: Synthesis across different benchmarks; not a formal meta-analysis. No large independent replication of any single headline number was found; most comparisons are within one paper by its authors.
agent_relevance: For the subgoal library: two-stage lookup (wide recall, then precision filter), union of lexical and learned rankings, scope filter, small final set, and a no-retrieval fallback.
